The Authentic Name

Why baꜥal.com is the correct form

Canaanite Original

Βαάλ

The name in its original Canaanite form. A name that carries the full phonetic weight of its source tradition.

ASCII Constraint

BAAL

Stripped of its identity, the name was reduced to plain Latin letters. The original orthography — stress, length, breathing — was erased by systems that only understand A-Z.

Unicode Restoration

Baꜥal

The Unicode restoration recovers what ASCII destroyed. This is philological accuracy — not decoration. The domain encodes to Punycode, but the browser displays the truth.

Valid Scholarly Variations
Baal Baʿal baꜥal Baál

Each variant is an attested scholarly orthography. The owned form is the active domain; others are historically valid alternatives.

Punycode Encoding
baꜥal.com → xn--baal-re8o.com

The non-ASCII characters in Baꜥal are encoded while the ASCII remains visible. To the DNS, it is Punycode. To humanity, it is Baꜥal.

04a

Unicode Registration Note

Why this flagship uses Egyptian Ain (ꜥ) instead of Semitic ʿayin

The historically accurate Semitic consonant in Baꜥal is ʿayin (ʿ), as attested in Hebrew ע, Phoenician 𐤏, and Arabic ع. However, the DNS root zone does not permit U+02BF (modifier letter reversed glottal stop) or the Arabic/Hebrew letter forms in domain labels. The only registrable Unicode workaround that preserves the phonetic identity of the consonant is Egyptian Ain (ꜥ, U+A725).

This substitution is purely a registry-level encoding constraint; it does not change the meaning, pronunciation, or Semitic sound structure of the name. The ideal form Baʿal is still acknowledged in the Etymology section above.

07

Mythology & Lore

The Canaanite storm king

Baꜥal Hadad is the storm god of the Ugaritic Baal Cycle — rider of the clouds, wielder of lightning, and bringer of the rains that make the Levant fertile.

Baꜥal’s great myth is a succession drama. He battles Yam, the sea, and defeats him with divine weapons forged by Kothar-wa-Khasis. After the victory, the high god El grants Baꜥal a palace on Mount Saphon (modern Jebel Aqra), the cosmic mountain.

Later, Baꜥal descends to the underworld and is killed by Mot, the god of death. The world withers until his sister ꜥAnat avenges him and restores him to life. This death-and-return pattern makes Baꜥal a deity of seasonal renewal — a Near Eastern parallel to figures like Dumuzi, Osiris, and even later dying-and-rising gods.

Because baʿlu simply means “lord,” many local gods were addressed as “Baal of” a place: Baal of Peor, Baal Zebub, Baal Hammon, and others.

08

Pronunciation

How to say the name

Reconstructed: /ˈbaʕal/ with a voiced pharyngeal fricative (ʿayin) in the middle.

The first syllable is ba; the second begins with the ʿayin, a sound made at the back of the throat — deeper than a glottal stop. English speakers often approximate it as “Bah-ahl.” The registrable form Baꜥal preserves the visual shape and phonetic identity using Egyptian Ain.

10

Syncretism

Baꜥal across cultures

Greek interpretatio: Philo of Byblos and other ancient sources identify Baꜥal / Hadad with Zeús. The storm-god of the Greeks and the storm-god of the Levant map onto each other naturally.

Roman world: Baꜥal was equated with Jupiter; in North Africa, Baal Hammon was syncretized with Saturn. The Roman Saturnalia may carry echoes of old Canaanite agricultural rites.

Hebrew Bible: Baꜥal appears as a rival deity to Yahweh. The name was later distorted into Beelzebub (“Lord of Flies”), a demonized figure in Jewish and Christian tradition.

Modern culture: “Baal” remains one of the most recognizable names from the ancient Near East, appearing in games, fantasy literature, and occult imagery.

11

Cultural Legacy

From Canaan to pop culture

The Baal Cycle is the single most important source for Canaanite religion. It shaped how scholars understand the world against which early Israel defined itself.

Baꜥal’s imagery — storm, bull, mountain, dying-and-rising — left traces in biblical poetry, in later demonology, and in the way Mediterranean cultures imagined divine kingship. The name itself, meaning simply “lord,” never disappeared; it was simply reassigned to new lords.
